en: The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-pañcavargika-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kasmira and others during the Song dynasty.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Of the month of spring, one night has passed, and only one night remains."
The moon is waning; old age and death are drawing near, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
Venerable sirs!
For the sake of attaining the Path, apply yourselves with single-minded diligence and vigor.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through single-minded and diligent application of energy; how much more so for other dharmas of the wholesome path!
"The one who has not yet received full ordination has already departed; what should the Sangha do first now that it is in harmony?
One person replied, "We shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts."
"Venerable sirs! The bhikṣus who have not arrived shall announce their *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*.
One person replied:
The discourse on desire is concluded.
Joining the ten fingers and palms in reverence, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas.
Now I wish to recite the precepts; may the Saṃgha listen with a single mind.
Even regarding minor offenses, one’s mind should feel great dread;
having committed a fault, repent with single-mindedness, and never commit it again.
The horse of the mind gallops down evil paths; when heedless, it is difficult to restrain.
The Buddha has taught all the precepts and practices, Just like a sharp bridle and rein.
When the Buddha’s mouth speaks these exhortations, Those who are virtuous can believe and accept them.
Such a person is like a well-trained horse; They are able to defeat the army of afflictions.
If one does not accept the instructions, nor takes delight in the precepts,
this person’s horse is untamed and they are submerged in the army of afflictions.
If a person guards the precepts as a yak loves its tail, [they will be well-restrained].
Binding the mind with heedfulness, like a monkey bound by chains,
always exerting oneself day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom—
such a person within the Buddha’s Dharma is able to attain a pure livelihood.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today is the fifteenth day for the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts; the Saṃgha shall perform the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts with a unified mind.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: let us together perform the *poṣadha* with a unified mind."
Thus it is announced.
"Venerable sirs! Now, for the uposatha, we shall recite the Prātimokṣa. Let everyone listen together and reflect upon it well."
If there is any offense, it should be confessed; those who are without offense remain silent.
By remaining silent, you should know that I and the venerable elders are pure.
As the Noble Ones remain silent, so too am I and the venerable elders.
If a bhikṣu, having been thus summoned before the assembly up to three times, remembers that he has committed an offense but does not disclose it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
The Buddha has declared that the offense of intentional lying is an obstructive dharma.
"To reveal one's transgressions brings peace and happiness; to fail to reveal them causes the offense to deepen.
"Venerable sirs, the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra has been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard?"
A second and third time, it is likewise said: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent;
thus shall this matter be held. "Venerable sirs!..."
"These four *pārājika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:

'If a bhikṣu, while training together with the other bhikṣus in the code of discipline, should engage in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—without relinquishing his feeble commitment to the precepts, that bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.'"

"If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given with a thieving mind—such that a king or a high minister should seize him, bind him, execute him, or banish him, saying: 'You are a thief!
You are a petty man! You are a fool! [he commits an offense]."
"Such a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.

If a bhikṣu, whether toward a human being or one resembling a human being, kills them himself, or provides a weapon or poison to kill them, or instructs another to kill them, or instructs them to commit suicide, praising death and extolling it, saying:
'Alas, man! What is the use of living this evil life?'"
"Death is better than life.
With such a thought, he follows his intention and kills; through various causes and conditions such as these, the person dies because of him.
That bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
"If a bhikṣu, without knowing or seeing the superhuman states, the noble benefits, and the fulfillment, claims of himself: 'I know thus; I see thus.'"
Later, whether that bhikṣu is questioned or not, for the sake of emerging from his offense and seeking purification, he speaks thus:
"I said I knew what I did not know, and I said I saw what I did not see; it was empty, deceptive, and false speech."
"Except in the case of overweening pride, this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion. "Venerable sirs!
The four pārājika dharmas have been recited."
If a bhikṣu violates any one of these precepts, he may not live in communal residence; as it was before, so it is after.
This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in communal residence with the others.
"Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
A second and third time he speaks thus: "The venerable ones are pure in this matter, for they are silent; thus shall this matter be held."
“Venerable sirs! These thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*.
‘If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except during a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.’”

"If a bhikṣu, his mind transformed by the intensity of lust, makes physical contact with the body of a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her hair, or grasping and rubbing any individual part of her body against its smoothness—it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, his mind transformed by the intensity of lust, addresses a woman with coarse and wicked words, speaking according to the ways of sexual desire, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, his mind transformed by the intensity of lust, praises his own person to a woman, saying: 'Sister!'"
“Sensual desire as an offering is the foremost offering.
This is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

“If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between, whether for a private liaison or otherwise, taking a man’s intention to a woman or a woman’s intention to a man, even to the extent of a single act of intercourse, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.”

"If a bhikṣu should beg for materials to build a hut for himself when there is no donor, it should be built according to the prescribed measure: twelve spans of the Buddha’s cubit in length and seven spans in width."
One should have the monks seek out a site for construction; the monks should indicate a site that is free from obstacles and has sufficient space for movement.
If one does not have the monks seek out a site, or if one constructs it beyond the prescribed dimensions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"If a bhikṣu, having a patron, builds a dwelling for himself, he should seek out a site for construction with the other bhikṣus.
Those bhikṣus should point out a site that is free of difficulties and has space for walking."
If he does not seek out a place for the bhikṣus [to investigate], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu, out of an improper and malicious anger, slanders a bhikṣu who is free from a *pārājika* offense with groundless charges of a *pārājika*, desiring to destroy that person's holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
If, at a later time, whether questioned or unasked, that bhikṣu says:
"This matter of mine was groundless; I slandered out of a state of anger," it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

"If a bhikṣu, out of improper and malicious anger, takes a portion or something resembling a portion from a different category and accuses a bhikṣu who has not committed a pārājika offense of having committed a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy that person's holy life."
At a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣu says:
"In this matter, I took a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a different category; I slandered him because I was dwelling in anger."
Saṃghāvaśeṣa. “If a bhikṣu exerts himself with skillful means to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha,
and the other bhikṣus say to that bhikṣu:”
"Do not exert yourself in means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha.

Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, it is joyful and free from contention; being of one mind and one training, like water and milk mixed together, you shall jointly propagate the Teacher’s instruction and dwell in peace and happiness."
If, despite being thus admonished, he persists and does not relinquish [the matter], he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, he relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu assists in the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha—whether there be two, three, or many—and says to the other bhikṣus:

'What this bhikṣu speaks is spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge; he speaks the Dharma, not what is not Dharma; he speaks the Vinaya, not what is not Vinaya; all of this is what our hearts accept and delight in.'"
The bhikṣus said to that bhikṣu: "Do not speak these words:

'What this bhikṣu has spoken was spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge; he spoke the Dharma and did not speak what is not Dharma; he spoke the Vinaya and did not speak what is not Vinaya; all of this is approved and welcomed by our own minds.'"
Why is this? This bhikṣu does not speak with knowledge; he does not speak the Dharma, nor does he speak the Vinaya.
You should not take pleasure in assisting in the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha; you should instead take pleasure in assisting in the harmony of the Saṃgha.

‘Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, they rejoice without contention; with one mind and one training, like water mixed with milk, they together propagate the Teacher’s instruction and practice in peace and happiness.
If, despite being admonished in this way, he persists and does not relinquish [his position], a second and third admonition should be given.
If, after being admonished a second and a third time, he abandons this matter, it is well;
if he does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu is of an evil nature and difficult to converse with, and repeatedly commits offenses while studying the sūtras and precepts together with the other bhikṣus."
When the bhikṣus admonish him for his transgression in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he replies:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak to me of what is good or bad; I shall likewise not speak to you of what is good or bad."
The bhikṣus spoke to him again, saying:
"Do not act as one who is 'uncommunicative with oneself.
You should speak according to the Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus shall likewise speak according to the Dharma for your sake."
"In this way, by teaching one another in succession and helping one another emerge from their offenses, they shall become the Saṃgha of the Tathāgata.
If, despite being thus admonished, he persists and does not relinquish his position, a second and third admonition should be given.
Second and third times, it is well if he abandons this matter;
if he does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, residing in dependence upon a village, engages in evil conduct and defiles the families of others..."
"It is seen, heard, and known that you have committed evil deeds; it is also seen, heard, and known that you have defiled families.
The bhikṣus say to that bhikṣu:
'You have committed evil deeds and defiled families.'"
"We have seen, heard, and known that you have committed evil deeds; we have also seen, heard, and known that you have defiled families.
You must depart; you should not remain here. That bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sirs, you are acting out of favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear. Why is this?
There are bhikṣus who have committed identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not."
The bhikṣus spoke to him again, saying:
"Do not speak these words:
'The Venerable Ones follow after desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.'"
"There are bhikṣus who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not.
You have practiced evil conduct and defiled the families of others.
Your practice of evil conduct has been seen, heard, and known; your defilement of the families of others has also been seen, heard, and known.
"You must abandon these words spoken out of attachment, aversion, delusion, or fear.
Depart from here; you should not remain in this community.
If, despite being admonished in this manner, he persists and does not relinquish his position, he should be admonished a second and a third time.
"Second and third times, it is well if he abandons this matter upon being admonished;
if he does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. O Venerable Ones!"
The thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas have been explained: nine are offenses at the first instance, and four require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these rules and knowingly conceals it, he shall be granted the *parivāsa* penance for as long as that period of concealment lasted.
Having completed the *parivāsa*, one undergoes the *mānatva* for six nights; next, one reaches the *ābṛhaṇa*.

Once this has been performed according to the Dharma, one should be cleared of the offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) before an assembly of twenty monks. If there is even one person less such that the number does not reach twenty, that bhikṣu shall not be cleared of the offense, and the other bhikṣus should reprimand him in accordance with the Dharma.
This is the nature of this Dharma.
Now I ask: "Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
A second and third time he speaks thus: "Since you are silent, venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter; let it be held as such."
“Venerable sirs! These two *aniyata-dharmas* (undetermined rules) are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
‘If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place suitable for sexual intercourse.’”

If a trustworthy female lay follower sees [an offense] and declares it according to each of the three categories of dharma—whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*—[the monk is deemed guilty].
If a bhikṣu says,
"It is as the upāsikā has stated," he should be dealt with according to what was stated among the three rules.
This is the first *aniyata-dharma*.
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place and speaks coarse, lewd words concerning sexual desire,
and a trustworthy *upāsikā* sees it and reports it according to one of two rules— either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*."
If a bhikṣu says,
"It is as the upāsikā has said," he should be dealt with according to whichever of the two rules she has stated.
"These are the two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas). Venerable sirs,
the two indeterminate rules have been recited."
Now I ask: "Are the Venerable Ones pure in this matter?
A second and third time it is said thus: "The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter; because of their silence, it shall be so held."
“Venerable sirs! These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*.
‘If a bhikṣu, having finished his three robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* cloth, keeps an extra robe for up to ten days...’”
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

"If a bhikṣu, having finished [making] his three robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe, should stay apart from any one of the three robes for even one night, except by formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*) of the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If a bhikṣu, having finished his three robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he needs it, provided he makes it up quickly and takes formal possession of it."
If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, one may hope for further acquisition from another source to make it complete, even for up to one month.
If this period is exceeded, it constitutes an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."

"If a bhikṣu begs for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except when there is a specific cause, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika). A 'specific cause' refers to:
having one's robes stolen, having one's robes lost, having one's robes burned, having one's robes carried away by water, or having one's robes destroyed; these are called specific causes."
"If a bhikṣu, having had his robes taken away, lost, burned, carried away by water, or destroyed, should beg for robes from a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative."
If a layman or a housewife wishes to give many robes, this bhikṣu should accept two robes; if he accepts more than this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative has planned together, saying, 'We shall use this amount for cloth to make a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu'—"
Without having first been invited by the householder or the householder’s wife, that bhikṣu went to them and asked, saying:
"Will you have a robe made for me with such an amount of money for cloth?"
He replied, “It is so. Then he said:
"Excellent, householder and housewife!
You may make such garments for me, so that they may be fine.
This constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If non-related laymen or laywomen have deliberated together, saying:
'We shall each provide the price for such robes to have them made, and give them to a certain bhikṣu.'"
"Before having been invited by his own free will, that bhikṣu went to the householder or the householder’s wife and asked them,
'Will you each make a robe for me using such an amount of money for robe-cloth?'"
He replied, "So it is. Then he said:
"Excellent, householder and housewife!
You may join together to make one robe for me, so that it may be fine.
This constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a king, a high minister, a brahmin, or a householder, for the sake of a bhikṣu, sends a messenger with the value of a robe.
The messenger arrives at the bhikṣu's place and says:
'Venerable sir!'"
"The king and his ministers have sent this payment for the robe;
Great Virtue, please accept it. The bhikṣu said:
"I should not accept the payment for the robe."
"If you obtain a pure robe, you should receive and maintain it with your own hands.
The messenger said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Is there anyone in charge?
The bhikṣu then pointed out the location.
The messenger went to the place where the person in charge was and said:
"A certain king or minister has sent the price for this robe to be given to a certain bhikṣu;
you should receive it and have it made.
He then gave it to him.
Having given it to him, the messenger returned to the bhikṣu and said:
"Venerable Sir!
I have already finished giving the item to the person in charge whom you indicated."
"Venerable sir, you need robes; you may go and take them.
That bhikṣu went to the person in charge two or three times and said: "I need robes."
"I require robes.
If he obtains them, that is well.
If he does not obtain them, he should go before the steward four times, five times, or six times, and stand there in silence.
If she obtains it, it is well.
If she seeks it beyond what is permitted and obtains it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she does not obtain the robe, she should go to the place from which the messenger came, either going herself or sending a messenger, and say:
"You were to deliver the price for robes to a certain bhikṣu, yet that bhikṣu did not receive them at all.
You must go back and retrieve it yourself; do not let it be lost.
This matter should be handled in this way."
"If a bhikṣu personally begs for thread and hires a weaver to weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a householder or a householder’s wife, for the sake of a bhikṣu, instructs a weaver to weave a robe..."
Without having first been invited by the weaver, that bhikṣu went to the weaver’s workshop and said this: "Do you know?
This robe is being made for me."
"Please weave this well for me, making it extremely fine and wide; I shall reward you separately.
If, afterwards, he gives her a meal or the value of a meal, and she accepts it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu, having given a robe to another bhikṣu, later becomes angry and displeased, and either takes it back himself or causes another to take it back, saying:
'Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
“[This constitutes] a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
‘If a bhikṣu, knowing that a donor intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it for his own personal use, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.’”
"If a bhikṣu is ill, he may take four kinds of medicinal substances for internal consumption:
ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
Having accepted them once, he may keep them for up to seven days."
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu is staying in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) during the three-month rains retreat before the eight months are complete, and if there is danger at that location, he is permitted to entrust each of his robes to a layperson within the boundary."
If there is a cause or condition for one to go outside the boundary, one may stay apart from this robe for up to six nights.
If it exceeds that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when one month of spring remains, should seek a rain-bathing robe, he should keep it for the remaining half-month."
If one seeks [the robe] less than one month before [the end of the retreat] but holds it for more than half a month, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, during the preceding or subsequent period of the rainy season retreat, when ten days remain before the *pravāraṇā*, receives a robe offered in haste, he may accept it if he requires it."
If the time for [receiving] robes has passed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when his bowl has not yet reached five mends, begs for a new bowl for the sake of its excellence, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
This bowl should be relinquished within the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should take the lowest-quality bowl from among the assembly and give it to him, saying:
"You shall accept this bowl until it breaks."
"This is the nature of this Dharma.
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl for up to ten days, and if it exceeds that period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If a bhikṣu..."
If a monk makes a new bed or mat from new *koseyya* (silk) fibers,
it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk makes a new bed or mat from pure black sheep's wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool from a ram, a third part white, and a fourth part inferior wool.”
If one exceeds this limit in making [a new bed or chair], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or seat, he should keep it for six years.

If, before the six years are complete—whether he has discarded it or not—he makes another new bedding or seat, except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-karman*), it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana* out of pure black sheep’s wool, he must use one Sugata-span of an old *niṣīdana* to spoil its fine color."
If he does not relinquish it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu obtains wool that he needs to carry and has a destination to reach, he may carry it himself for up to three *yojanas*."
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool from a ram, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade for the sake of profit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu buys and sells gold, silver, or money in various ways, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu himself takes hold of gold, silver, or coins; or causes another to take them; or forms the intention to accept them, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. "Venerable sirs!"
The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas have already been recited.
Now I ask: "Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
A second and third time it is asked in the same way: "Since there is silence, the venerable sirs are pure in this matter; thus shall this matter be held."
"Venerable sirs! These ninety-one *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
'If a bhikṣu speaks a deliberate falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
“If a bhikṣu reviles another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu engages in double-tongued speech to cause strife and discord among bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.”

"If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except when there is a man present who understands the distinction between what is wholesome and unwholesome speech, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha has finished a legal matter according to the Dharma, should reopen it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu teaches a sūtra to a person who has not yet received full ordination and recites it together with them, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not yet received full ordination for more than three nights, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, toward one who has not yet received full ordination, speaks of having attained a superhuman state, saying:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
If it is true, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), speaks of it to one who is not yet fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (*saṃghakamma*), it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣu speaks thus: ‘What is the use of these minor rules of training?
When these rules are recited, they cause people distress and vexation.’”
"Whoever thus reviles the precepts commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu cuts down a 'village of spirits' (a grove of trees) himself, or causes another to cut it down, he commits a *pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu intentionally fails to answer when questioned, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu falsely accuses a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu, having personally spread bedding belonging to the Saṃgha on an open space, or having had someone else spread it, or seeing it spread by another, sits or lies down upon it, and when departing does not lift it up himself, nor instruct another to lift it up, nor entrust it to someone to be lifted up; or if he sees bedding belonging to the Saṃgha spread on an open space and fails to lift it up, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu, having personally spread bedding belonging to the Saṃgha within a monastery cell, or having had someone else spread it, or seeing that another has spread it, sits upon it or lies down upon it, and when departing does not himself put it away, nor instruct another to put it away, nor entrust it to someone to be put away, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, personally drags a bhikṣu out of a monastery dwelling, or causes another to drag him out, saying:
'Get out! Begone! Do not stay here.'"
“[This constitutes] a *pāyattika*.
‘If a bhikṣu, knowing that another has already spread bedding, later comes and forcibly spreads it himself or causes another to spread it, thinking:
“If he does not like it, he shall leave of his own accord.”’”

“An *pāyattika*. “If a bhikṣu, on an upper story of a multi-storied building belonging to the Saṃgha, sits or lies down forcefully upon a corded bed or a wooden bed with pointed legs, it is an *pāyattika*.

“If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, he may pile [the foundation] from level ground, leaving space for windows and doors, making it as solid as possible, and providing two or three layers of roofing.”
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living creatures, takes it for the purpose of pouring on mud, or for food, drink, or other uses, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣu, not being appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs bhikṣuṇīs, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
“If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, [continues] until sunset, it is an offense of expiation.”
"If a bhikṣu, without being appointed by the Saṃgha, enters the dwelling place of bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of instructing them, except in cases of illness, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu speaks thus: 'The bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of gain and offerings,' [it is a pāyattika]."
"Pāyattika. 'If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded, private place with a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a pāyattika.'"
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for another, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having made a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī, travels together with her along a road from one village to another, except for a legitimate reason, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the "circumstances": if one has many companions or is in a place where there is suspicion or fear, these are called circumstances.
"If a bhikṣu, having made a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī, travels together by boat—whether going upstream or downstream—with the exception of crossing directly across, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the cause of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, should eat it—except when a donor has previously made a resolution to give—it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly [at different times], except for [appropriate] causes, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the "circumstances": the time of illness, the time of [receiving] robes, and the time of being offered robes—these are called the circumstances.
"If a bhikṣu accepts a separate invitation for a communal meal, it is a pāyattika offense, except in the case of the circumstances."

The "causes and conditions" are: the time of illness, the time for robes, the time for the distribution of robes, the time for making robes, the time of traveling on a road, the time of traveling by boat, the time of a great assembly, and the time of a gathering of śramaṇas; these are called causes and conditions.
"If a bhikṣu, when not ill, stays at a place where a single meal is offered and takes more than one meal, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson who freely offers much food and drink, whether cakes or parched grain..."
If one does not eat at that person's house, one should accept two or three bowls and go outside to eat together with other bhikṣus.
If one is not ill, to accept more than this or to eat without sharing with other bhikṣus constitutes a pāyattika offense.
“If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, does not perform the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-vidhi), it is a pāyattika.

“If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished his meal and has not performed the ritual for leftover food, forcibly urges him to eat with the intent to cause him to commit an offense, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu places food into his mouth that has not been formally received, except for tasting food, tooth-sticks, and water, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu eats leftover food from a previous night, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a naked ascetic, whether male or female, it is a pāyattika.”
"If there is such fine food in a household—
namely milk, curd, ghee, fish, or meat—
and a bhikṣu who is not ill seeks it out for his own sake and obtains it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a house where food is being served, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu sits alone in a secluded place with a woman, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu goes to observe an army on its march, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu has a reason to go among the military forces, he may stay for two or three nights at most.
If he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu has a reason to go among the military forces and stays for two or three nights, yet observes the military array or the engagement of battle, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu should speak thus:
'As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, the dharmas that obstruct the path cannot actually obstruct the path,' the other bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:"
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Buddha, do not misrepresent the Buddha.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha as being obstructive to the Path truly does obstruct the Path.
You must abandon this evil and false view."
If, after being admonished in this manner, he persists and does not relinquish it, he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If he relinquishes the matter, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has not repented according to the Dharma and has not abandoned his evil and false views, sits with him, speaks with him, sleeps with him, or associates with him, it is a pāyattika."
"If a śrāmaṇera should speak thus:
'As I understand what the Buddha has taught, one who indulges in the five desires cannot be obstructed in the Path,' the bhikṣus should say to that śrāmaṇera:"
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Buddha, do not misrepresent the Buddha.
The Buddha has taught that the five desires obstruct the Path and truly can obstruct the Path.
You, Śrāmaṇera, must abandon this evil and heterodox view."
If he thus instructs him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish it, the instruction should be repeated a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third instructions, he relinquishes this matter, it is well.
If he does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should say to that śrāmaṇera:

"Go away! From this day forth, do not say that the Buddha is your teacher; do not walk behind the bhikṣus. While other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with bhikṣus for two nights, you have no such privilege."
"Foolish man, get out! Be gone! Do not stay here.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled according to the Dharma, nevertheless keeps him, employs him, or dwells and converses with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu intentionally causes another bhikṣu to feel doubt or regret, thinking:
'I shall cause that bhikṣu to be troubled, even if only for a short time.'"
“A *pāyattika*. “If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is conducting its business, rises and leaves without having given his consent (*chanda*), it is a *pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣu tickles another bhikṣu, it is a *pāyattika*.”
“If a bhikṣu plays in water, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu treats his teacher or the precepts with contempt, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth himself, or causes another to dig it, saying: 'Dig!'"
...this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu is engaged in a dispute and listens in silence, thinking:
'I shall remember what the bhikṣus say.'"
"An offense of expiation (pāyattika).
If a bhikṣu knowingly confers full ordination upon one who is less than twenty years of age, it is an offense of expiation.
This person does not obtain the precepts, and the other bhikṣus may also censure him."
This is the nature of the Dharma:

"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for medicine for four months, and if he accepts beyond this period—except in the case of a renewed invitation, a personally delivered invitation, or a long-term invitation—it is a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu repeatedly commits offenses, and the other bhikṣus admonish him in accordance with the Dharma, he says:
'I will not study this precept; I shall ask other bhikṣus who are upholders of the Dharma and the Vinaya.'"
[Otherwise, it is] a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu wishes to seek clarification, he should question those who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya.
This is how the law ought to be.
"If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, should say:

'I have only now learned that this rule was spoken in the half-monthly *poṣadha* sūtra,' and the other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has already sat through the recitation of the precepts two or three times, that bhikṣu cannot escape on the grounds of ignorance; he shall be dealt with according to the law in accordance with the offense he has committed."
One should reprove him for his ignorance and for his unwholesome conduct.
If, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, one does not listen with a single-minded focus or does not take them to heart, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu enters beyond the threshold of the inner palace while the king has not yet departed and the treasures have not yet been stored away, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu agrees to travel along a road with a thief from one village to another, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu agrees to travel along a road with a woman from one village to another, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu, when not ill, lights a fire for the purpose of warming himself, or causes another to light it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
“If a bhikṣu takes up, or causes another to take up, a jewel or an object equivalent to a jewel, except within a monastery or a lodging, he commits a pāyattika offense.”
If one takes precious objects or the like within a monastic dwelling or at a lodging, and a claimant for them appears later, they should be returned.
This matter should be handled in this way.
"If a bhikṣu bathes within a half-month, except for a legitimate cause, it is a pāyattika offense."
Regarding the "causes and conditions": they are the time of illness, the time of work, the time of travel, the time of wind and rain, and the time of heat; these are called causes and conditions.
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger, makes a threatening gesture with his hand toward another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu intentionally terrifies another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it for more than one night, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, with groundless charges of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, slanders another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Come together to various households; I will give you much delicious food and drink,' and having arrived there, does not give it to him, saying: [he commits an offense]."
"Go away! It is not pleasant for me to sit or speak with you; it is pleasant for me to sit alone and speak alone.
If, wishing to cause him distress, one says this, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must mark it with one of three colors: blue, black, or madder-brown.
If he does not mark it with these three colors, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika)."
"If a bhikṣu, for the sake of amusement, hides another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case,
or any such individual article of daily use, or causes another to hide it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is deciding a matter, has already given his consent in accordance with the Dharma, yet later censures it,
it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu speaks thus: 'The bhikṣus distribute the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal acquaintances,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having given a pure gift of robes to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, takes it back, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation for a meal before or after [the midday meal], goes to another household without informing a nearby bhikṣu, except when there is a valid reason."
*Pāyattika*. Regarding the "circumstances": the time for robes is what is meant by "circumstances.
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without approaching a virtuous bhikṣu to inform him, except when there is a [valid] circumstance, it is a *pāyattika*."
Regarding the "causal condition" (*nidāna*): in times of difficulty, this is called the causal condition.
"If a bhikṣu makes a sitting or reclining mat stuffed with *tūla* (cotton down), it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu himself makes a rope bed or a wooden bed for sitting or reclining, the legs should be eight fingers high according to the measure of the Sugata, excluding the portion inserted into the frame."
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), it should be made according to the prescribed measure: two *śugata-vidatthi* in length, one and a half *vidatthi* in width, with an additional square of one *vidatthi* for the border."
If it exceeds this, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu makes a wound-covering robe, he should make it according to the proper measure: four Sugata-spaṣṭas in length and two spaṣṭas in width."
If it exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, he should make it according to the proper measure: five Sugata-spans in length and two and a half spans in width."
If he exceeds [the measure], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe of the measure of a Sugata’s robe, or exceeds it, it is a *pāyattika*.
The measure of a Sugata’s robe is nine Sugata-spans in length and six spans in width; this is called the measure of a Sugata’s robe."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a donor intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it to another person, it is a pāyattika.
"Venerable sirs! The ninety-one pāyattika dharmas have been recited."
Now I ask: "Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
A second and third time he speaks thus: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent; thus I shall hold it to be so."
"Venerable sirs! These four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
'If a bhikṣu, being not ill, receives food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative while in a street or alleyway.'"
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones.
This is called the dharma of confession.
"If a monk has been invited to a meal at a layperson's house, and a bhikṣuṇī instructs the person serving food, saying:
'Give rice to this monk; give soup to this monk.'"
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Step back for a moment and wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
If not even a single person among the assembly speaks, those bhikṣus should confess their transgression to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones."
This is called the method for repenting a transgression.
"There are families under training (*śikṣamāṇa-kula*) upon whom the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of designating them as families under training.
If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, has not previously received an invitation, yet accepts food with his own hands from such a family under training..."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression to the venerable ones.
This is called the dharma of confession.

"If a bhikṣu, while staying in a forest hermitage where there is apprehension or fear, does not first scout the area, yet accepts food with his own hands within the monastery or does not go outside to receive it."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones.
This is called the dharma of confession.
"Venerable sirs! The four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas have been recited.
Now I ask: Are you pure in regard to these matters?"
A second and third time, it is said in the same manner: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent;
thus do I hold it to be so. "Venerable sirs!..."
These are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma) recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra:
"One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe too high.
One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe too low."
"One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe unevenly.
One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe like a palm leaf.
One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe like an elephant's trunk."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not put on my inner robe so that it is rounded like a pomegranate.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not hold the inner robe too tightly.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear the upper robe too high.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not put on my robe in a manner that hangs down.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not put on my robe unevenly.
One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the dwellings of householders while properly covering my body.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the dwellings of laypeople with my body properly covered and seated.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the dwellings of laypeople with my robe tucked back over my right shoulder.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe folded back and placed over my right shoulder.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe folded back and placed over my left shoulder.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe draped over one shoulder in a reversed manner.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe draped over both shoulders in a reversed manner.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the dwelling of a layperson with my robe tucked up at the sides and draped over both shoulders while seated.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the dwelling of a layperson swaying the body.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson while swaying the body.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson while shaking the head.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson while shaking the head.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not swing my shoulders when entering the home of a layperson.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit with swinging shoulders in the home of a layperson.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the home of a layperson with hands clasped together.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with hands joined.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson in secret.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson in secret.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with hands on hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with hands on hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson resting my cheek [on my hand].'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my cheek resting on my hand.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with swinging arms.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with swinging arms.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with a gaze cast upward.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with a gaze cast upward.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson while looking left and right.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson while looking left and right.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson walking in a crouching posture.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson walking in a crouching posture.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson walking on tiptoe.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson walking on tiptoe.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my head covered.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my head covered.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson in a playful or laughing manner.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson in a playful or laughing manner.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the homes of laypeople without raising my voice.
One should train oneself: 'I shall sit in the homes of laypeople without raising my voice.
One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the homes of laypeople with composed and dignified decorum.'"
"One should train in sitting with composure in the homes of laypeople.
One should train in receiving food with a single-minded focus.
One should train in receiving food without overflowing the bowl."
"One should train oneself: 'One shall eat both the soup and the rice together.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat from various places within the bowl.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not scoop out the center of the food to eat.'"
"One should train oneself not to eat by wiping the bowl with a bent finger.
One should train oneself not to eat while sniffing at the food.
One should train oneself to look attentively at the food in the bowl."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not discard food.
One should train oneself: 'With hands soiled by food, one shall not grasp a vessel for pure food.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not slurp while eating.'"
"One should train oneself not to make noise while eating.
One should train oneself not to lick the bowl.
One should train oneself not to take up a full handful of food."
"One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat with the mouth wide open.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not wait with the mouth wide open when the rice has not yet arrived.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat while wrinkling the nose.'"
"One should train oneself not to speak while eating.
One should train oneself not to stuff the cheeks while eating.
One should train oneself not to bite off half a morsel."
"One should train oneself not to reach out with an extended arm to take food.
One should train oneself not to shake one's hand while eating.
One should train oneself not to protrude the tongue while eating."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not swallow food whole.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not clump rice together and hurl it into my mouth from a distance.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sprinkle water containing food from my bowl onto the floor of a layperson's house.'"
"One should train oneself not to cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more.
One should train oneself not to disparage or criticize the food.
One should train oneself not to request additional food for one's own sake."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not look at the bowl of my neighbor with a mind of aversion.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not defecate or urinate into pure water, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself not to defecate or urinate upon living grass or vegetables, except when ill.
One should train oneself not to preach the Dharma to a person wearing wooden sandals, except when ill."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one wearing leather sandals, except in cases of illness.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who exposes their chest, except in cases of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is seated and a bhikṣu is standing, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is on a high seat and a bhikṣu is on a lower seat, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is lying down and a bhikṣu is sitting, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is in front and a bhikṣu is behind, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is on the road and a bhikṣu is off the road, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'One should not preach the Dharma to a person with their head covered, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to one who has wrapped their robe over one shoulder, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to one who has wrapped their robe over both shoulders, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has covered their body with a cloak.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is riding on a mount.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one leaning on a staff, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one holding a sword, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to one who is holding a bow and arrow, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not climb a tree higher than a person's height, except for a weighty reason.'"
"Venerable sirs! The rules of training for the multitude have been recited.
Now I ask: Are you pure in these matters, venerable sirs?"
"A second and third time it is said thus: 'Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent;
thus do I hold this matter. Venerable sirs!"
These seven methods for settling disputes are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
"One should grant the *vinaya* of presence; one grants the *vinaya* of presence.
One should grant the *vinaya* of mindfulness; one grants the *vinaya* of mindfulness."
"One should grant the *amūḍhavinaya*; grant the *amūḍhavinaya*.
One should grant the *pratijñākāraka*; grant the treatment of the *pratijñākāraka*.
One should grant the *svavāda*; grant the treatment of the *svavāda*."
"One should grant the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*; one should grant the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*.
One should grant the *tṛṇaprastāra*; one should grant the *tṛṇaprastāra*. Venerable sirs!"
The seven methods for settling disputes have already been explained.
Now I ask: "Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
A second and a third time he speaks thus: "Since you are silent, venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter; let it be held as such."

"Venerable sirs! The introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra has been recited; the four pārājika rules have been recited; the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules have been recited; the two aniyata rules have been recited; the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules have been recited; the ninety-one pāyattika rules have been recited; the four pratideśanīya rules have been recited; the śaikṣa rules have been recited; and the seven adhikaraṇa-śamatha rules have been recited."
This Dharma is included within the Buddha’s Sūtra on the Precepts, recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa, as well as other precepts that follow the Path.
Regarding these, you venerable ones, with a single mind in harmony, rejoicing and without dispute—like water mixed with milk—should train yourselves in dwelling in peace and happiness.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa for the Saṅgha of those seeking tranquility:
"Patience is the supreme path; Nirvāṇa is declared by the Buddha to be the foremost.
One who harms others while claiming to have left the household life Is not called a śramaṇa."
“Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the peaceful Saṅgha, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
‘Just as a person with clear vision Is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths, So too,
a wise person in this world Is able to distance themselves from all evils.’”
"Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of those seeking tranquility, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
'Not harming others, nor speaking ill of them, Acting in accordance with what is taught in the precepts, Knowing moderation in eating and drinking, Always delighting in dwelling in seclusion. "
"With a mind tranquil, joyful, and diligent—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa for the Saṅgha of the Tranquil:
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Without harming its color or fragrance,"
Take only its flavor and depart;
do not disrupt another's affairs, nor consider what has been done or left undone.
Observe only your own bodily conduct, and examine closely what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
“Kanakamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the saṅgha of those seeking tranquility, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
‘If you wish to attain a virtuous mind, do not be negligent; You should diligently train in the noble Dharma.
If there is one who knows tranquility and possesses a unified mind, Then they shall no longer have sorrow or affliction.’”
“Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the silent Saṅgha, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
‘Commit no evil whatsoever; Fully cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
Thoroughly purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas.’”
“Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of the Peaceful, has briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
‘To guard the body is good; to guard the speech is also good;
to guard the mind is good; to guard all [the sense-faculties] is good.’”
The bhikṣu who guards all [the senses] shall be freed from all suffering.
The bhikṣu who restrains his speech and mind, and whose body commits no evil,
purifies these three paths of action and attains the path realized by the noble ones.
If one is struck or reviled and does not retaliate, if one harbors no resentment toward those who hate,
and maintains constant tranquility within a heart of anger, seeing others do evil, one does not do it oneself.
“The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who were able to rescue and protect the world, have fully expounded the precept-sūtra which they taught; I have now completed its detailed exposition.
All Buddhas and their disciples revere this precept-sūtra.”
"Having paid respect to the Sūtra on the Precepts, and having shown mutual respect to one another,
being fully endowed with shame and remorse, one is able to attain the unconditioned path. "Venerable sirs!"
The Prātimokṣa has now been fully recited; the Saṃgha, being of one mind, has performed the Poṣadha.
Regarding this *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-pañcavargika-śīla-sūtra* in one fascicle: the National Edition (Guoben) agrees with the Song Edition, while the Dan Edition alone differs.
How should one decide which to accept?
Examining this now against the original Vinaya, it is clear that this edition from Dan (the Northern Wei) is the correct one.
Those editions from Guo and Song are actually the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* found within this "Sui" (隨) case, translated by Kumārajīva.
The text was mistakenly rewritten as the *Pañcavargika-prātimokṣa*, yet it was attributed to Buddhayaśas.
Although there are minor discrepancies therein, these are merely errors of transcription; therefore, this edition from Danzhou has now been selected for inclusion in the canon.
